projects.title: Three-statement model and DCF valuation of a listed company
projects.summary: Pick a real listed company, rebuild three years of its income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement from its annual report (10-K), forecast five years from clear drivers, and value it with a DCF and a sensitivity table.
projects.why: Financial modeling is the skill most finance job offers ask for, and the hardest to prove without experience. A clean, linked model of a real company, with a balance sheet that balances and a valuation you can defend, gives you something concrete to show and to talk about in technical interviews.

data.name: SEC EDGAR full-text search
data.note: Find the company and download its last three annual reports (10-K): the statements and the notes.

data.name: Damodaran Online, current data
data.note: Industry betas, cost of capital, equity risk premium and multiples by industry, updated every January.

data.name: FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)
data.note: The 10-year Treasury yield (series DGS10) for the risk-free rate.

steps.title: Choose the company
steps.text: Pick a listed company with a simple business that files a 10-K: one or two segments, no bank or insurer (their statements work differently). Read the business section and write down in three sentences how it makes money.

steps.title: Rebuild the historical statements
steps.text: Enter three years of income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement in Excel, one tab each, in the company’s own line items grouped into a standard layout. Check that the balance sheet balances and that the cash flow statement ends on the balance sheet cash every year.

steps.title: Set the drivers
steps.text: On an assumptions tab, compute the historical ratios (revenue growth, gross and operating margin, capex and depreciation as % of revenue, receivable, inventory and payable days, tax rate) and choose five years of forecast values, each with a one-line reason taken from the 10-K or the industry.

steps.title: Link the forecast
steps.text: Forecast the income statement from the drivers, then the balance sheet (working capital from the days, PP&E from capex and depreciation, debt from its schedule) and the cash flow statement. Cash comes from the cash flow statement; add a check line that the balance sheet balances in every year.

steps.title: Value it with a DCF
steps.text: Compute unlevered free cash flow, then the WACC: risk-free rate from FRED, industry beta and equity risk premium from Damodaran, cost of debt from the interest expense and debt, weights from market values. Add a terminal value (perpetual growth), discount to enterprise value, subtract net debt and divide by diluted shares.

steps.title: Test and present
steps.text: Build a sensitivity table of the share value on WACC and terminal growth, compare with the share price and with the industry multiples, and write a one-page note: value range, the three assumptions that matter most, and what would change your view.

deliverables: The Excel model: historicals, assumptions, linked forecast, DCF and sensitivity tabs
A one-page valuation note with the value range and key assumptions
A short list of sources (10-K pages, FRED series, Damodaran tables)
A README on GitHub or a portfolio page with screenshots
checklist: The balance sheet balances in every historical and forecast year
Cash on the balance sheet comes from the cash flow statement, not a plug
Inputs are in one colour and on one tab; no hard-coded numbers in formulas
Every forecast driver has a written reason
Free cash flow is unlevered: EBIT after tax, plus D&A, minus capex and the increase in working capital
The terminal growth rate is below long-term nominal economic growth
Net debt and diluted shares are taken from the latest 10-K
The note gives a range and the sensitivities, not a single exact price

cv.bullet: Built a linked three-statement model and DCF of [company] from its 10-K filings (personal project): 5-year driver-based forecast, WACC of [x]% from market data, value range of [$a–$b] per share with sensitivity analysis.
cv.talk: Walk through how one driver, for example receivable days, flows through the three statements to free cash flow, then explain which assumption moves the value most and why you chose your number.

stretch: Add a downside and an upside scenario with a switch on the assumptions tab.
Cross-check the DCF with a comparable companies valuation (EV/EBITDA, P/E) on four peers.
Model the impact of a share buyback or a new loan on earnings per share and leverage.

projects.title: Monthly budget vs actual pack with a price, volume and mix bridge
projects.summary: Turn Microsoft’s financial sample data into the monthly management pack an FP&A team sends: a budget, actual vs budget by product and country, a price / volume / mix bridge that explains the gap, and a rolling forecast for the rest of the year.
projects.why: Budget vs actual reviews and forecasts are the daily work of FP&A analysts and controllers. A pack that explains a variance with a clear bridge and a written comment shows you can do more than build a table: you can tell management what happened and what comes next.

data.name: Power BI financial sample
data.note: A free Excel workbook of sales by segment, country, product and month: units, prices, discounts, cost of goods sold and profit.

data.name: Principles of Managerial Accounting (OpenStax)
data.note: A free textbook: budgeting, standard costs and variance analysis, to check your method.

steps.title: Load and check the data
steps.text: Load the workbook into Power BI or Excel (Power Query), set the data types, and check the totals: gross sales minus discounts equals sales, sales minus COGS equals profit. Note the months and years covered.

steps.title: Build the budget
steps.text: Write a budget for the last year of the data from the year before: volumes by product and country with a growth assumption, budget prices and discount rates, and budget unit costs. Keep the assumptions on one sheet so anyone can see and change them.

steps.title: Compare actual with budget
steps.text: Build the actual vs budget table by month, product, country and segment for units, sales, gross margin and margin %, with the variance in value and in %, and a year-to-date view.

steps.title: Explain the gap with a bridge
steps.text: Split the sales variance into volume (change in units at budget price and mix), mix (change in product mix at budget prices) and price (change in net price times actual units). Check that the three effects add up exactly to the total gap, and show them in a waterfall chart.

steps.title: Add a rolling forecast
steps.text: From a chosen month, replace the remaining budget months with a forecast built from the latest actual run rate and your assumptions, so the pack always shows the next 12 months. Compare the full-year forecast with the budget.

steps.title: Write the commentary
steps.text: Write the comment a manager would read first: the headline numbers, the two or three causes of the gap with their amounts, whether each is timing or permanent, the full-year outlook and the actions to propose.

deliverables: The Power BI report or Excel pack: summary page, actual vs budget, bridge and forecast
The assumptions sheet for the budget and the forecast
A README with screenshots and the variance formulas you used
checklist: Your totals match the source workbook
Budget assumptions are written down and kept apart from the formulas
Variances have a clear sign convention (favourable / unfavourable)
Volume, mix and price effects add up exactly to the total variance
The waterfall starts at budget and ends at actual
The rolling forecast always shows the next 12 months
The commentary gives amounts, causes and actions, not only percentages
The summary page fits on one screen

cv.bullet: Built a monthly budget vs actual pack in [Power BI / Excel] on [N] months of sales data (personal project): price / volume / mix bridge explaining a [x]% revenue variance, 12-month rolling forecast and management commentary.
cv.talk: Explain how you split the variance into volume, mix and price, show that the effects add up to the total gap, and read your commentary as if presenting it to a manager.

stretch: Add a cost of goods sold bridge (volume and unit cost effects) to explain the margin variance.
Add a scenario switch (low, base, high) to the rolling forecast.
Track forecast accuracy month after month and show where your assumptions were wrong.

projects.title: Peer comparison of listed companies from SEC XBRL data
projects.summary: Pull five years of reported figures for four or five listed companies in one sector from the SEC’s free XBRL APIs, compute margins, returns, working capital and leverage ratios with Python or SQL, and write a comparison of who performs best and why.
projects.why: Financial analysts compare companies all the time, and more and more job offers ask for Python or SQL on top of Excel. Building the dataset yourself from official filings, and turning the ratios into a clear story, shows both the analysis and the data skills.

data.name: EDGAR application programming interfaces
data.note: Free JSON APIs on XBRL data: companyfacts (all reported figures of one company) and frames (one figure for every company in a period).

data.name: Kaggle Learn: Pandas
data.note: A short free course on the pandas operations you need: selecting, grouping, reshaping.

data.name: SEC EDGAR full-text search
data.note: Find each company’s CIK number and check a figure against the 10-K when a value looks odd.

steps.title: Choose the sector and peers
steps.text: Pick one sector and four or five companies of similar business model that file with the SEC (for example retailers, software or airlines). Write down why they are comparable and their fiscal year ends.

steps.title: Download the data
steps.text: Call the companyfacts API for each company’s CIK (declare a User-Agent with your name and email, as the SEC asks, and stay under its rate limit). Save the raw JSON so your work can be re-run.

steps.title: Build a clean table
steps.text: With pandas (or load into SQLite and use SQL), keep the annual 10-K values (form 10-K, fiscal period FY) of the tags you need: revenue, gross profit, operating income, net income, total assets, equity, current assets and liabilities, receivables, inventory, debt, cash, operating cash flow and capex. Companies use different tags for the same item: map them, and drop duplicates from later filings.

steps.title: Compute the ratios
steps.text: Compute revenue growth, gross, operating and net margins, return on equity and on assets, current ratio, receivable and inventory days, net debt to EBITDA or to equity, and free cash flow margin, for each company and year.

steps.title: Check the numbers
steps.text: Check two figures per company against the 10-K itself, look for gaps and outliers (a merger, a change of year end, a one-off), and note what you adjusted or excluded.

steps.title: Tell the story
steps.text: Present a few charts and a ranking table, then a one-page write-up: who is most profitable, who converts profit into cash best, who carries the most risk, and the business reasons you found in the 10-Ks.

deliverables: The notebook or SQL scripts that download, clean and compute everything
A clean CSV of the figures and ratios by company and year
Charts and a one-page comparison write-up
A README on GitHub explaining the tags, the mapping and how to re-run it
checklist: The companies are really comparable, and you said why
Only annual 10-K values are used, with no duplicated years
Tag mapping is written down for each company
Two figures per company match the published 10-K
Each ratio has a written formula
Outliers and one-offs are explained, not silently removed
The write-up explains the business reasons behind the ratios
The SEC fair access rules were respected (User-Agent, rate limit)

cv.bullet: Compared [N] listed [sector] companies over 5 years from SEC XBRL data with [Python / SQL] (personal project): automated download, [N] financial ratios (margins, returns, working capital, leverage) and a written peer analysis.
cv.talk: Explain one difference you found between two peers, for example in working capital or margins, the ratio that shows it and the business reason behind it, then how you made sure the data was right.

stretch: Use the frames API to place your peers in the distribution of the whole sector for one ratio.
Add a DuPont breakdown of return on equity (margin, asset turnover, leverage).
Publish the ratios in a small Power BI or Streamlit dashboard refreshed from the API.
